https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_s_.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania‘s National Alliance eyes 2028 breakthrough as support holds at 4–5 percent 2026-07-20 Linas Jegelevicius According to the latest 2026 polls, Lithuania’s National Alliance (NS), a nationalist and conservative party emphasizing sovereignty, national identity, and immigration control, is hovering around the threshold for entering the Seimas, the country‘s Parliament, with about 4–5 percent support. The Baltic Times Magazine asked NS Chairman and MP Vytautas Sinica to answer the questions. Why do you think your party is not seeing stronger public backing? I believe there are many reasons why we are not growing faster. The main one is visibility. I am the only National Alliance representative in the Seimas. I think I am relatively visible and heard, but I am still only one person. I had to fight for media attention, and I believe I succeeded. Compared to the 2024 election period, my favorable ratings have tripled, while the party's ratings have roughly doubled. This is particularly noticeable in Vilnius, where we receive over 8% support and, according to polls, are the city's third-largest party. Not long ago, nobody would have imagined that. In addition, we lost the first year of this parliamentary term due to internal party problems. The leadership changed in a painful way, and I was even expelled from the party before later becoming its chairman. This frightened and disappointed some of our supporters, and we had to regain their trust. Since we resolved those issues and I became chairman, we have seen continuous growth. Our stated goal for the 2028 elections is to surpass the 5 percent threshold. If we continue growing at the current pace, it appears we will exceed that goal by a considerable margin. There is an evident competition on Lithuania's political right between your National Alliance (NS), TS-LKD, Nemunas Dawn and the prospective party of MP Ignas Vėgėlė. Which parties do you believe have the strongest prospects, and why? I would not agree that we are all competing for exactly the same voters. As a political scientist, I am convinced that Lithuanian voters are primarily divided by their attitude toward national defense: whether they believe defense should be strengthened, more money should be allocated to it, and other sacrifices should be made, or not. Cultural and economic issues come only afterward. From this perspective, the National Alliance competes with TS-LKD, while Nemunas Dawn competes with Vegele – or rather, will compete if he actually establishes a viable political party. I would not venture to predict who will perform better. TS-LKD will certainly remain one of the largest parties in the next elections, and we do not yet expect to surpass them. However, expectations that Laurynas Kasciunas becoming party chairman would make TS-LKD more conservative and more national-minded are fading. The party has not changed and continues to marginalize its more conservative members. I am convinced that the National Alliance is the only party genuinely fighting to preserve a Lithuanian Lithuania – its borders, language and nation – not only against military threats but also against cultural disappearance. Vegele’s prospects will largely depend on Nemunas Dawn: whether it can convincingly position itself as an anti-establishment force while in opposition. If it cannot, opportunities will open up for Vegele. Which legislative packages or amendments have you managed to pass with the support of other members of the Seimas? Which of your legislative initiatives would you highlight, and why? During my first year, I was more pleased with successfully stopping harmful initiatives than passing new ones. These included proposals concerning the Law on National Minorities, amendments to the Equal Opportunities Law, an international labor convention, civil partnership legislation, and the expansion of so-called hate speech penalties. Unfortunately, we failed to stop the expansion of the real estate tax and what I consider excessively burdensome building requirements for homes in Lithuania. Most of my own legislative initiatives focus on immigration control. So far, the Seimas has approved at the initial stage my proposals to tighten deportation rules for foreign nationals who commit crimes and to grant border guards greater authority to revoke residence permits. It is also worth mentioning that the Seimas approved, at the introductory stage, my proposal for a referendum on the definition of the family. More than 60 members of parliament signed the initiative. Unfortunately, Julius Sabatauskas has been delaying its progress in committee. How much has National Alliance membership and the number of regional branches increased since the 2024 parliamentary elections? During the first year after the elections, the party experienced internal difficulties, and membership actually declined, falling below the legally required threshold of 2,000 members. Since last autumn, however, membership has been steadily increasing. Around 200 new members have joined during this period. In addition, five new regional branches have been established. We hope to create several more this year. Lithuanian society, like many other democratic societies, is deeply polarized. In your view, what ideas or initiatives could unite the country and its people? Where should such initiatives come from? All societies are united by their perception of external threats. In Lithuania, the objective and very significant threat posed by Russia undoubtedly plays a unifying role. We may disagree about the best means of responding to that threat, but a large majority of society recognizes its existence. Migration is another external challenge that, in my view, should unite the nation, although this is not yet as widely understood. Conversely, what divides society the most are cultural and values-based conflicts – debates over family, gender, language, abortion and similar issues. A responsible government that genuinely seeks to unite society should avoid provoking such disputes and, in particular, should not pursue policies that run counter to the views of the majority on these issues. That is the most direct path toward social tension. I hope – and I am doing everything I can in the Seimas – to ensure there is enough wisdom to avoid creating such conflicts. Photograph: Aaron Chown/PA Prince Harry Prince Harry and Meghan ‘moving back to Britain this month’ Reports say Duke and Duchess of Sussex intend to relocate from US, with children to start British school in September Nadeem Badshah Wed 19 Aug 2026 17.48 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 19.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to return to live in Britain, six years after leaving for the US, it has been reported. The couple and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate later this month to a non-royal residence. The property is believed to be outside London, and the children are enrolled to start school in September, the Daily Telegraph reported. King Charles was informed on Sunday that his son and daughter-in-law would return to Britain, according to the Telegraph. It comes after the Sussexes, who have lived in California since 2020, had a reunion with the king last month at Highgrove in Gloucestershire. The king is said to welcome the opportunity to see more of his family in a personal capacity but there will be no change in their status as private individuals after relinquishing their official working roles within the royal family. The Prince and Princess of Wales are said to have also been informed of the decision. The couple are expected to retain their homes in Montecito, California, and Portugal, where they went on holiday earlier this summer. The duke and duchess’s security arrangements have not been disclosed. The long-running issue over their security meant that Prince Harry did not bring Meghan, 45, or their children to events in London last month, as had been originally planned. Prince Harry, 41, has previously stressed he would not feel safe bringing his family back to the UK without police protection. In May 2025, after losing a legal challenge over his security in the UK , the Duke of Sussex said: “I can’t see a world in which I would bring my wife and children back to the UK at this point.” In an interview with the BBC after the ruling, Prince Harry said he “would love a reconciliation” with the royal family. He said: “There have been so many disagreements between myself and some of my family,” but he had now “forgiven” them. “I would love reconciliation with my family. There’s no point continuing to fight any more, life is precious.” Prince Harry added the dispute over his security had “always been the sticking point”. Asked whether he had asked the king to intervene in the dispute over security, he said: “I never asked him to intervene – I asked him to step out of the way and let the experts do their jobs.” Last month, the Duke of Sussex and six other co-claimants lost their privacy case against the publishers of the Daily Mail in London . The claimants, who included Doreen Lawrence and Elton John, sued Associated Newspapers Ltd over allegations of unlawful information gathering. Their claims were dismissed in their entirety by Mr Justice Nicklin. https://hungarytoday.hu/the-magyarabs-of.text: The Magyarabs of Wadi Halfa: Hungary’s Forgotten Tribe in Africa Hidden along the Nile near Wadi Halfa, in the borderlands of Egypt and Sudan, lies a remarkable community whose traditions are said to preserve the memory of a distant Hungarian past. Known as the Magyarabs, they trace their ancestry to Hungarian soldiers who were reportedly brought to Nubia in the 16th century and settled there as border guards. Centuries later, their story came to the attention of Hungarian explorer László Almásy, who encountered the community during his 1934 expedition. László Almásy, t he Hungarian explorer who inspired The English Patient , was one of the most renowned figures in Hungarian African exploration. He is credited with discovering the Zarzura Oasis and the Cave of the Swimmers, as well as mapping a significant portion of the Sahara. He is said to have been the first European and Hungarian to encounter members of this community. The encounter took place during a motor expedition to Nubia (southern Egypt and northern Sudan) in 1934–1935. In the memoirs of Henry Cecil Jackson, Governor of Sudan, it was noted that while traveling from Sudan toward Egypt, near Wadi Halfa, Count Almásy noticed that the local people were speaking a language reminiscent of Hungarian. After asking where they were from, he learned that they lived on the island of Magyar-narki, whose name means “the island of the Hungarians.” Almásy described the details of this encounter—including his conversation with the Hungarian Arabs living on an island in the Nile near Vádi Halfa and with representatives of the tribe—in his book “In the Air… on the Sand…” (originally titled in Hungarian as Levegőben, homokon ), published in 1937. Almásy learned that the ancestors of the Magyars had been settled there more than 400 years earlier by Sultan Selim II as border guards. Almásy had to continue his journey to Cairo, where he received documents detailing the history of the Magyars. After his departure, Hansjoachim von der Esch continued researching the history of the Magyars in Wadi Halfa. On the island of Magyararti, he collected about 150 Hungarian words, and the people told him: We men are descended from the Hungarian people; nothing about our past has ever been recorded in books, but we have preserved our history and still know very well today where we came from.” Based on his literary research, Esch discovered that Sultan Selim I invaded Egypt in 1517 and brought captive men from Slavonia, Syrmia, Transylvania, and Bosnia, who found a home there after the fighting ended. Their leader, Ibrahim al-Magyari—that is, Ábrahám Magyar—remained there with 20–25 cavalrymen, and they married local women. From this union, Ibrahim al-Magyari had a son named Musa, who also married a local girl, and the Hungarian tribe of Wadi Halfa is said to trace its origins to them. The population of the Magyars is estimated at 30,000–40,000. The broader historical context is also notable: in 1516, Gábor Pécsváradi, a Franciscan monk, personally spoke with Hungarians serving in the Turkish army passing through Jerusalem, which he also recounted in a letter addressed to János Bánffy, the royal cupbearer. The monk spent 33 months in the Holy Land and recounted his experiences in a book titled Journey to Jerusalem. The next Hungarian expedition reached the village of the Magyars in 1965. István Fodor, the distinguished Arabist and interpreter, spent several months in Wadi Halfa during the flooding that preceded the construction of the Aswan High Dam. He researched the history, behavior, customs, and culture of the Magyar people, as well as their attitudes toward Hungarians and their Hungarian heritage. In addition, he collected proverbs such as “Ál-Mágyárí lá jiszálli fíl-meszgyid,” meaning “A Magyar does not pray in the mosque.” This saying dates back to the time when the Magyars were still Christians. But here is another proverb: “Rá’sz el-mágyár zejj el-hágyár,” meaning “the Hungarians’ heads are as hard as stone,” and another one: “the Magyars wear hats.” Magyar women carve a cross into raw Nubian bread before placing it in the oven. They also draw a cross on the foreheads of newborns, even though they converted to Islam long ago. Prior to the Second Congress of the World Federation of Hungarians, the organization’s then-president, Sándor Csoóri, was asked to recognize the Magyarabs into the World Federation. Sándor Csoóri sent them a certificate of admission and three plane tickets so that their representatives could attend the congress. When they received the certificate, their eyes filled with tears, and they said, “We are honored by the invitation, but we do not need the plane tickets, because we are not poor people.” They came to Budapest nearly 500 years later, as if they had never left. Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/Reuters Indonesia Indonesian police investigate deaths of Australian man and two children in Bali as suspected murder-suicide Police in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own life Caitlin Cassidy Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.44 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life. The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning. According to Denpasar police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at about 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach. Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar police said in its statement. The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located. “Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read. “From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.” The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Central general hospital for further examination and handling. The Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta police officers were investigating the incident. “Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said. Simatupang said Kuta police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate. A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians. “We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement. Skip next section After 10 years, India introduces UPI charges for merchants 09/16/2026 September 16, 2026 After 10 years, India introduces UPI charges for merchants According to government data, India had 554.9 million UPI users as of June [FILE: October 28, 2022] Image: Payel Samanta/DW Ten years after the launch of the popular instant digital payment system Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the Indian government announced charges on transactions on Tuesday. However, the charges will only be on merchants and payments between two individuals remain free. The charges, known as the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), are taking effect from October 15. According to the government circular: Person-to-person UPI payments will remain free regardless of the amount Merchant payments of up to ₹2,000 (€18.06) will also remain free. Merchant transactions above ₹2,000 will have 0.4% MDR levied MDR will be capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh (€903) a month through UPI will continue to pay zero MDR Sectors such as railways, fuel and telecommunications will have a flat ₹5 fee for transactions above ₹2,000. Last month, the Indian parliament passed a bill allowing the government to levy charges on UPI. According to the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the MDR framework will enable further investment in "infrastructure resiliency, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service." As of June, India had 554.9 million UPI users , according to NPCI. Meanwhile, UPI transactions worth ₹29,82,355.95 crore (about €269.3 billion) were recorded in August, NPCI data showed. According to India, a Pakistani naval ship approached its warship at high speed, causing a collision on Tuesday in international waters. No major damage was reported. The Indian ship was on a routine surveillance mission, officials said. "The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to ​convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions ​of the relevant agreements between the ‌two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," the ministry said. India said the incident violated a 1991 agreement requiring the countries' naval vessels and submarines to maintain a distance of at least three nautical miles in international waters. Pakistan has not issued a statement regarding the incident. This incident marks the first overt military tension between the nuclear-armed rivals since their four-day conflict last year, which threatened to turn into a full-blown war . https://p.dw.com/p/5MgNi Skip next section US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India 09/16/2026 September 16, 2026 US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India India-US ties could come under pressure as the US lawmakers consider a Russia sanctions bill that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. India, a major consumer of Russian energy, could be affected by the measure. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in a 214-211 vote, media reports said. The House is expected to hold a final vote on Wednesday. The bill, imposing sanctions on Russia's leadership, energy and defense sectors and "shadow fleet" accused of helping Moscow evade oil sanctions, was passed by the Senate last month. If approved by the House, the bill would go to Trump to be signed into law. The proposed tariffs seek to increase economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy. India-US ties facing test While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil . Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff. However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework. However, the landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough.
